children: By Elizabeth Bernstein
I had to put my dog down last month.
She was my beloved sidekick for almost 13 years, and her death left me heartbroken. I felt as if I'd lost my best friend.
I also felt isolated in my grief. Although friends and family reached out to offer condolences, their lives quickly moved on. Yet mine had a huge hole in it.

Psychologists have a name for this experience: "disenfranchised grief." When a pet dies, there are no formalized rituals, mourning periods or bereavement leaves. Not everyone recognizes the importance of the loss or is supportive. It can be very lonely.
"People aren't comfortable talking about their grief over an animal because they are worried about being judged," says E.B. Bartels, author of "Good Grief: On Loving Pets, Here and Hereafter."
Yet pets eat, sleep and snuggle with us and are privy to our emotions. They're childlike in their dependence. For many people, their dog, cat or other pet is their sole source of daily companionship.
A beloved animal's death can also bring up grief over other losses — a late loved one; a relationship that didn't endure; our former self.
"When a pet dies, we lose a witness to an era of our life," Bartels says.

I asked readers of my column how they coped with pet grief and heard from dozens. Some talked to AI about their loss, created videos, paintings and poems as memorials or got a new pet to help fill the void.

A television producer in Miami keeps the ashes of his beloved Brussels griffon on his nightstand. A retired school administrator and author in Los Angeles included a picture of himself with his husky-Saint Bernard on his jacket book. A social worker in Delray Beach, Fla., held a pet-supply drive and donated the haul to a local shelter after losing her poodle.

A nonprofit executive in Washington, D.C., wrote a five-page letter to her late black mouth cur explaining her grief, guilt and gratitude. "I've reread that letter multiple times and can still feel the relief and healing that writing it provided me," she says.
Here are other standout strategies:
Take your grief seriously
Acknowledge it. Cry. Take time off work. Talk about it or join a pet-grief support group.
Beth Berry made the painful decision to euthanize her 12-year-old goldendoodle, Jesse, last month after the dog's cancer metastasized. "My world stopped," she said.
To cope, she created a group chat of friends who loved Jesse. She also joined several pet-grief support groups. Helping others through their grief helped, she says.
And she allows herself to cry or step away from work briefly to meditate. "I give myself grace," says Berry, 63, who works in hotel operations. "Grief is not linear."
Don't feel guilty

People often blame themselves when a pet dies, especially if they chose euthanasia, says Marla Bennett, a psychologist in Jacksonville, Fla., who specializes in the human-pet bond. She recommends focusing on the whole relationship, not just the end.

Veterinarian Kate Elden of San Diego has guided many people through a pet's death. Yet when Cody — her 15-year-old Labrador-golden retriever and best man at her wedding — died in 2019, she was overcome with guilt. Elden, 41, had let Cody visit her dad in the mountains while she worked. She beat herself up for not examining the dog beforehand or being there when he died.
She grieved for years, crying through euthanasias and when a dog reminded her of Cody. Then she finally decided to take her own advice.
"You make the best decisions you can for your pet, with their best interests at heart and the information you have in that moment," says Elden.
Choose a ritual
Write an obituary. Have a funeral. Make a memorial.

When his 18-year-old Shih Tzu, Jack, died in 2024, Rick Chretien and his family held a celebration of life. Chretien chose a spot in the garden where Jack loved to roam to inter his ashes. His adult children, who grew up with the dog, wrote a eulogy and made a list of songs to play ("You've Got a Friend in Me" made the cut.) His wife poured wine for the toast. Everyone cried.
"It helped us be at peace with losing him," says Chretien, 67, a retired vice principal from Manchester, N.H.
And now he has another source of solace: a new Shih Tzu named Leo.
Be grateful
Reflect on how your pet expanded your world.
In February, Robert Emmons decided to euthanize his 11-year-old golden retriever, Joey, after learning hours earlier that the dog was critically ill. His grief was "staggering," he says.

To cope, he wrote a list of 10 specific ways the dog had enriched his life — the memories, adventures and moments that made him belly laugh. He prefaced each item with the words: "I am grateful to remember..."
The practice brought him a "profound peace," says Emmons, 68, a retired psychology professor in Scarborough, Maine. "Grief is simply gratitude in another form."
Grieving Scout
I made the gut-wrenching decision to put Scout down with very little notice.

Years ago, I bought a sterling-silver charm for her collar engraved with her name and "MVP" for Most Valuable Puppy. I joked that she had jewelry. But I knew that the charm was really for me when she was gone. After I said goodbye, I began wearing it on a necklace.
For days, I sensed her presence around the house — crunching kibbles, barking at the front door, pressing against me in bed. It was comforting.

I also scrolled through endless photos; wrote her obituary; and traded stories about her with my niece and nephews, who loved her. And I kept talking to her, just as I had throughout our days together. I told her what I was doing, how much I missed her, and what she'd taught me.
That's when it struck me: She's not really gone, even if I can't cuddle with her. She's here, in my heart, forever.
